subject: Lighthouse private cluster: evacuation, SSD fallback, and node-slice plan
messages:
From: Samir Khan <samir@lighthousehealth.com>
To: Jordan Blake <jordan_blake@redwood.ai>, Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.ai>
Cc: Angela Ruiz <angela.ruiz@lighthousehealth.com>
Date: Tue, 06 Jul 2027 15:12:00 -0700
Subject: Planning: on-prem cluster — evacuation and SSD fallback questions

Hi Jordan / Marissa,

Thanks again for the walkthrough today. We took notes on the overall architecture but need a short written plan to present to our infra team and CISO. Main asks: can you outline how Redwood recommends handling zero-downtime node evacuation for maintenance, and what the sanctioned fallback is if our NVMe cache saturates (local SSD spillover vs remote blockstore)? Angela is concerned about data durability during maintenance windows and how snapshot/backup cadence interacts with eviction.

I've attached a current node inventory (Lighthouse_NodeInventory.xlsx) to show the node types we plan to provision. High-level constraints:
- Two racks per site, each with mixed CPU + small GPU nodes
- Local NVMe on all inference nodes (fast cache) and 1TB SATA SSD for longer-lived spills
- Strict change freeze between 03:00-08:00 local time; maintenance must be staged to avoid clinical windows

Could you share a short checklist and the node-pool + storage-class recommendations we should propose to our SREs? Also flag any network egress or peering items we should include for the security review.

Thanks,
Samir
Samir Khan
Director, Platform Ops
Lighthouse Health Systems

[Attachment: Lighthouse_NodeInventory.xlsx (application/vnd.openxmlformats-officedocument.spreadsheetml.sheet)]

From: Jordan Blake <jordan_blake@redwood.ai>
To: Samir Khan <samir@lighthousehealth.com>
Cc: Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.ai>, Irene Choi <irene_choi@redwood.ai>
Date: Wed, 07 Jul 2027 09:30:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Planning: on-prem cluster — evacuation and SSD fallback questions

Samir — thanks for the inventory and the clear constraints. Below is a concise plan you can share with Lighthouse SREs; I'll follow up with a short runbook draft and a MAP (mutual action plan) from Marissa.

1) Cluster topology (high level)
- Control plane: 3 dedicated control-plane nodes per site (tainted, no workloads)
- System nodes: small footprint (logging, metrics, ingress) with local persistent storage for short-lived state
- Inference pool(s): separate node pools for CPU inference and GPU inference to control scheduling and binpacking
- Cache tier: inference nodes with NVMe (fast ephemeral cache) + a smaller persistent SSD class for spillover

2) Node-pool sizing and slice strategy
- Slice sizes: prefer uniform 8-12 node slices for autoscaler granularity (align to rack boundaries to reduce blast radius)
- Taints/tolerations: taint control-plane/system nodes; use dedicated taints for GPU pools to ensure correct scheduling
- PodDisruptionBudgets: enforce PDBs per critical service with minAvailable set to tolerate one node eviction per slice

3) Storage classes and durability model
- ephem-nvme (StorageClass): ReadWriteOnce + ephemeral local PV for cache (do not rely on this for durable state)
- ssd-spill (StorageClass): ReadWriteOnce provisioning on local SATA SSDs with replication via snapshot to central blockstore nightly
- central-block (StorageClass): ReadWriteMany on SAN/NFS for durable volumes (backed up nightly with weekly offsite snapshot)
- Binding mode: use WaitForFirstConsumer for spill volumes to ensure correct topology-aware provisioning
- Encryption: encrypt at rest for spill and central block volumes (customer KMS integration)

4) Evacuation and fallback pattern (zero-downtime guidance)
- Planned maintenance: cordon + drain with graceful termination; for critical pods use preStop hooks and extended terminationGracePeriod to avoid dropouts
- Evacuation order: start with system pods, then scale down inference slices one slice at a time, rely on PDBs to keep minimum traffic served
- NVMe saturation: set kubelet eviction thresholds (nodefs.available, imagefs.available) to trigger preemptive spill to ssd-spill class before eviction occurs
- SSD fallback: implement an operator/sidecar that checkpoints cache items to ssd-spill on high watermarks; this reduces cold-cache penalty during node churn

5) Backups, snapshots and RTO/RPO
- Snapshot cadence: cache-level snapshots (hourly) for ssd-spill; persistent volumes on central-block snapshot every 4 hours with 24h retention for dev/prod parity as needed
- RTO targets: aim for 15m for routing fallback and 60m for full cache warm-up; set customer expectations for warm-up cost/time

6) Networking and peering notes for security review
- Private peering: establish VPC peering with site-to-site tunnel and enforce strict egress rules at the network edge
- Service mesh: optional — recommend starting without mesh, advocate a CNI (Calico with BGP) for stable L3 routing and policy control
- Egress logging: enable flow logs and forward to Lighthouse SIEM for compliance

Next steps: Marissa will share a MAP + timeline; Irene will draft the maintenance runbook with exact kubectl commands and kubelet tuning suggestions. Irene — can you add the kubelet eviction/gc knobs and an evacuation checklist?

— Jordan
Jordan Blake
Head of Deployments, Redwood Inference

From: Irene Choi <irene_choi@redwood.ai>
To: Samir Khan <samir@lighthousehealth.com>, Jordan Blake <jordan_blake@redwood.ai>
Cc: Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.ai>
Date: Thu, 08 Jul 2027 08:45:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Planning: on-prem cluster — evacuation and SSD fallback questions

Samir — adding the technical knobs and a short checklist you can copy into the runbook. Paste below into your runbook and adjust thresholds per node sizing.

Kubelet / eviction / GC knobs (suggested):
- --eviction-hard=imagefs.available<5%,nodefs.available<10%
- --eviction-soft=imagefs.available<10%,nodefs.available<15% --eviction-soft-grace-period=imagefs.available=1m,nodefs.available=2m
- kube-reserved: cpu=500m,memory=1Gi for system daemons (adjust per host)
- system-reserved: cpu=200m,memory=512Mi
- eviction signal tuning: ensure local SSD is in separate mount to allow fine-grained thresholds

Evacuation checklist (per slice):
1) Announce maintenance window to stakeholders and disable clinical traffic route if necessary
2) Cordon target nodes: kubectl cordon <node>
3) Drain with graceful timeout: kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data --grace-period=120 --timeout=15m
4) Monitor PDBs and ensure minAvailable is maintained
5) If drain logs show imagefs pressure, trigger cache checkpoint to ssd-spill: 
   - POST /internal/cache-checkpoint (operator endpoint) 
6) After maintenance, uncordon: kubectl uncordon <node> and monitor rolling traffic

Network items to include for the security questionnaire:
- IP ranges for control plane and node pools (we recommend non-overlapping with corporate CIDR)
- BGP peering endpoints with redundancy across the two racks
- Flow logs retention policy and SIEM integration point

I'll attach a sample kubelet config diff and a minimal operator snippet for cache checkpointing in the next message.

— Irene
Senior Technical Program Manager, Redwood Inference
